bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 14: Successive Refinement (Case Study of a Command-Line Argument Parser)

question: How does a working but messy module become clean code, and what discipline makes that safe?
hypothesis: Clean code is reached by writing a rough draft and then refining it in many tiny test-protected steps, not by writing it clean in one pass.
contributions: A worked case study of refactoring the Args command-line parser from a rough draft to a clean design, with the stopping point and step sequence shown

results.claim: Clean code is not written in one pass: you write dirty code first and then clean it.
results.setup: Stated as the chapter's thesis
results.quote: programming is a craft more than it is a science.

limits: Single case, one author, one small module; no measurement of effort, defects or time (the 10 and 30 step counts are the only quantities).
Intermediate listings are partial; the author leaves the final transformations as an exercise (p. 250).
Relies on a pre-existing unit suite plus FitNesse acceptance suite written while building the messy version; the chapter does not show how to get tests onto untested code.
Java 2008-era code (ParseException, StringBuffer, Iterator, JUnit 3); the steps are language-neutral but the listings have dated.
practices: Write a rough draft and then clean it; do not expect clean code in one pass (p. 200).
Do not leave working code in whatever state it reached; this is 'professional suicide' (p. 201).
Stop adding features and refactor at the point where the next features would make the mess unfixable (p. 212).
Look for repeated parse/set/get shape across variants and introduce a class for the concept (p. 212).
Make many very tiny changes, each keeping the system working; never break the system (pp. 212-213).
Keep a fast automated suite you can run on a whim; run acceptance tests as well as unit tests (pp. 213, 224).
When a step breaks tests, fix it before the next change (p. 214).
Migrate by adding the new structure beside the old, switching users one at a time, then deleting the old (p. 221).
Replace a type-case with polymorphism by pushing each branch down into the subclasses (pp. 231-237).
Test extensibility: adding a new type should be few, isolated changes (p. 237).
Separate concerns by moving exception and error-message code into its own class (pp. 239-250).
Clean continuously; never let rot start (p. 250).

terms.definition: Writing a rough draft, then a second draft and several subsequent drafts until the final version; applied to code as dirty code then cleaned.
Making only changes that keep the system working as before, verified by tests.
